label: Qualitative properties of W2 gradient flows
notes: This chapter, printed pages 693 to 718, moves past existence to the qualitative behaviour of Wasserstein gradient flows. The unifying engine is displacement convexity: when the driving functional is K-convex along geodesics, the flow inherits contraction, uniqueness, stability, and exponential trend to equilibrium, all packaged inside one variational inequality.

label: From steepest descent to a flow
notes: Recall the heuristic: a Wasserstein gradient flow runs steepest descent of a functional on the metric space of probability measures. The minimizing-movement scheme builds curves of maximal slope, but a scheme alone gives no rates. We need a sharper differential characterization that survives the lack of smoothness in this metric setting.

label: K-displacement convexity
notes: The single hypothesis driving every result is lambda-convexity along displacement geodesics. With constant K, the functional lies above each chord by a quadratic correction tuned by the squared Wasserstein distance. Positive K means a genuinely convex landscape; negative K still controls the flow, only with weaker, possibly growing, estimates.

label: The Evolution Variational Inequality
notes: The EVI is the heart of the chapter. It states that along the flow the half time-derivative of squared distance to any test measure is bounded by the functional gap minus a K-quadratic term. This single inequality, holding for all comparison measures, encodes the whole qualitative theory at once.

label: Why EVI is the right notion
notes: EVI is stronger than being a curve of maximal slope: it is rigid enough to pin down a unique solution yet flexible enough to pass to limits. A flow satisfying EVI with parameter K is automatically a gradient flow of a K-convex functional, so EVI characterizes the dynamics completely.

label: Contraction between two solutions
notes: Apply EVI to each of two solutions, using the other as the test measure, and add. The functional terms cancel by symmetry, leaving a clean differential inequality for the squared distance between the trajectories. Gronwall then yields lambda-contraction: distinct flows can never spread apart faster than the exponential rate allows.

label: The contraction estimate
notes: The contraction estimate reads as exponential comparison of the two trajectories: their Wasserstein distance at time t is at most the initial distance times e to the minus K t. When K is positive the two flows are pulled together; when K is negative they may separate, but only at a controlled exponential rate.

label: Uniqueness and stability
notes: Contraction is not just elegant; it is the workhorse. Setting the initial data equal forces the two solutions to coincide, giving uniqueness. Letting initial data vary makes the solution map Lipschitz in the Wasserstein distance, so the flow depends continuously and stably on its starting measure with an explicit modulus.

label: Convergence to equilibrium
notes: When K is strictly positive the functional has a unique minimizer, the equilibrium measure. Taking that minimizer as the fixed test point in EVI turns contraction into exponential convergence: every flow relaxes to equilibrium in Wasserstein distance at rate K, with a matching exponential decay of the functional toward its minimum.

label: Visualizing exponential contraction
notes: The picture makes the algebra tangible. Two flow trajectories start apart, bend toward one another, and merge at the equilibrium measure, while the gap between them collapses along an exponential envelope. The decay curve is the geometric shadow of the EVI inequality acting between the two solutions.

label: Computational footprint
notes: In the companion notebook the theorem becomes inspectable: two smoothing density flows are evolved and their Wasserstein distance is recorded over time. The attached invariant simply checks that this distance curve is nonincreasing within tolerance, turning the abstract contraction statement into a Boolean that fails if the idea is misread.

label: Synthesis and outlook
notes: To close: one hypothesis, K-displacement convexity, produces the EVI, and the EVI alone yields contraction, uniqueness, stability, and exponential equilibration at rate K. Pages 693 to 718 thus turn qualitative folklore into a tight quantitative package that later chapters reuse for functional inequalities and concentration.
